study.title: Psalm 112 The fear of the LORD and the stability of the righteous
study.overview: This psalm describes the man who fears the LORD as a truly happy one, not by a momentary triumph, but by a life marked by obedience, generosity, inner firmness and lasting memory. The poem connects personal bliss to the good of the family, to the public reputation and to care for those in need. In the end, the destiny of the wicked contrasts with that of the righteous: as justice remains, the desire of the wicked is undone.

outline.title: The fear of the Lord and the blessing that reaches the house
outline.explanation: The psalm begins with a bliss: happy is he who fears the LORD and rejoices in his commandments. This fear is not a servile fear, but obedient reverence. The text highlights that the offspring of this man will be firm, and that his house will know provision and honor, showing that piety has effects that reach the family and the continuity of the generation.

outline.title: Godly character: light, mercy and stability
outline.explanation: From here, the righteous is described by his way of acting: he is godly, merciful, just, prudent and generous. Even in darkness, there is light for him, indicating divine direction in difficult times. His firmness does not depend on circumstances, because his trust is in the Lord, and therefore his name remains in lasting remembrance.

outline.title: Confidence before the opposition and final contrast with the perverse
outline.explanation: The righteous man does not live dominated by bad news or by the fear of enemies; his heart is established until he sees their defeat. He distributes to the needy, and his righteousness continues. In contrast, the wicked looks at this prosperity with irritation and envy, but ends up consumed, because his desires do not reach permanence.

study.context: The psalm is presented as a song of praise, attached to the former by the emphasis on the wisdom born of the fear of the LORD. The text is poetic and sapiential, that is, it teaches the way of life of the righteous through descriptions and contrasts. The notes provided also observe the alphabetical structure of the psalm, but the focus of the chapter, by the content itself, is in the life of the just and in its contrast to the perverse.
study.theology: Theologically, the psalm teaches that the fear of the LORD produces a life of joyful obedience, not of empty bondage. Justice here is not only a moral statement, but a concrete practice: mercy, prudence, generosity and trust. Divine blessing appears as inner stability, lasting memory and impact on the community and family. The psalm also states that the good of the righteous provokes opposition in the ungodly, but this opposition is temporary; justice remains, as long as the perverse desire perishes. In Protestant evangelical reading, this points to the centrality of a living faith that is expressed in works, without reducing these works to the cause of salvation.

scholarViews.insight: The righteous imitate God being generous, compassionate and upright; in the psalm, this includes lending to the poor without charging interest.
The happiness of the just includes stability and good reputation: it will not be moved forever, and his remembrance will remain.
It is not enough to fear God; it must also love him, and from this love is born joyful obedience to his commandments.

questions: Does my fear of the Lord appear in joyful obedience or just in religious language?
How are my home and resources being used to bless others, especially those in need?
Does my trust in God stand firm when rumors, opposition, or envy arise?
study.practice: Practise this week a concrete form of mercy: help someone in need, with prudence and without ostentation. At the same time, examine whether your confidence is in circumstances or in the Lord. Pray that your heart will stand firm and that your obedience may be joyful, not forced.
study.uncertainty: The notes of the commentators are interpretations and may differ among themselves; the biblical text is the main reference. The chapter alone does not safely inform dates, specific authorships or historical details beyond the poetic genre and sapiential tone. Nor is it possible to affirm with certainty, only on the basis of this material, whether all expressions about prosperity should be read strictly materialally or also spiritually.
